title: Breeding history, not dietary adaptation, drives growth of house crickets, Acheta domesticus (Orthoptera: Gryllidae), on novel feeds
content:
Abstract
Understanding how insect populations respond to novel diets is key to optimizing feed formulations and production efficiency in insect farming. In a controlled, replicated feeding trial, we reciprocally cross-fed 2 house cricket (Acheta domesticus (L.)) lines that had been maintained for >4 yr on distinct diets, a cereal‑based mix and a commercial formulation; the commercial-fed line had also been selected for larger body size. We partitioned growth into effects of diet adaptation (the advantage of the historical diet), diet composition and body-size selection. Mean body mass increased in all cages, and there was no evidence that survival differed among treatments. Line identity dominated growth: the commercial-fed line was more than twice as heavy at week 5 as the cereal-fed line, irrespective of feed (0.19 g; 95% CrI 0.12 to 0.25). The higher-fat commercial diet probably increased mass slightly in both lines (0.03 g; 95% CrI −0.02 to 0.10; Pr(effect > 0) = 0.87). In contrast, there was no evidence of a home-diet advantage on either an absolute or a proportional scale (0.003 g; 95% CrI −0.06 to 0.07; Pr = 0.55). Switching to a novel diet carried no detectable growth cost, suggesting physiological plasticity rather than diet adaptation. For producers, these results imply that line origin matters far more than the choice between these feeds. Future work should use replicated lines, follow crickets to harvest age at production densities, and combine feed‑intake measurements with microbiome analyses to separate consumption from conversion efficiency effects.
